51caa7cfc1:
This chapter covers what an architect decides about the model-facing part of a Claude solution:

  • which model tier handles each task, and how that is proved;
  • how the choice is revisited when a cheaper lever exists;
  • when to route or cascade, and why self-reported confidence is not a safe trigger;
  • how model identifiers and prompts are treated as versioned dependencies, with a release gate and a canary;
  • how a system prompt is structured, and how prompt templates become reviewed artifacts;
  • which rules belong in the prompt and which in code;
  • how zero-shot, few-shot and chain-of-thought techniques are chosen by measurement.

Every number in this chapter comes from a runnable example in the companion folder. Every price, latency and accuracy is an illustrative placeholder.
9563b68a3c:
The exam facts quoted in this guide (63 items, 120 minutes, a $175 fee, seven domains, a guide-authored practice scenario with a 95 percent per-type floor) come from third-party summaries of the CCAR-P blueprint. Treat them as a study map. Read the current official exam guide before you book.

This chapter also names product details that change: model identifiers, context-window sizes, prices, the names of the effort and thinking parameters, and which tiers support them. Where a detail matters I write "check the docs".

The prices in the examples ($1 and $5, $3 and $15, $5 and $25 per million input and output tokens for a small, mid and large tier) are placeholders. I chose them so the ratios are plausible. They are not quotes, and no accuracy or latency figure in this chapter was measured on a real model.
1c54838818:
The chapter fits in two sentences.

Every model-facing choice, which tier, which technique, which prompt, which rule sits where, is a decision made against a written per-segment requirement and a measured result, and the simplest configuration that passes every segment wins.

Because a model call is probabilistic and a prompt is configuration that changes behaviour, both are managed like any other production dependency: pinned, versioned, tested before release, rolled out to a slice of traffic, and reversible in one step, with hard rules enforced by code below the prompt.
f4b276a535:
Most of the rest is the working out.

The tier is chosen by a probe that reports accuracy for every segment, p95 latency and cost per call. You run the probe on the cheapest tier first. When no tier passes, the cause usually sits in the prompt, the labels or the requirement. So you pull the cheap levers first (prompt, effort, moving arithmetic into code), and the expensive one (a larger tier) last.

Mixed traffic is routed to the cheapest adequate tier. The router, or the acceptance check, is itself a classifier, and it gets evaluated too.

A system prompt is a sectioned, reviewed piece of configuration, with reasons attached to its rules. A template is a versioned artifact: it has a content hash, an approval that requires an evaluation, and callers that pin an exact version.

And the guardrails come in layers. The prompt reduces how often the model does something wrong. Only code makes it impossible.
fee55c12a8:
CCAR-P asks about all of this as judgement under constraints, not as parameter trivia. A typical item describes a care assistant, gives you three numbers (a volume, an SLA, a cost ceiling), and offers four designs.

The winning design does three things. It ties each choice to a number from the scenario. It picks the simplest option that clears every segment. And it keeps governance in the design.

This chapter builds that habit on a telecom running example: a voice self-service (IVR) classifier that has 800 milliseconds at p95. A retail returns assistant and a billing-credit assistant sit alongside it.
a58dda1990:
Scope and cross-references.

  • Chapter 05 owns the context window itself: token budgets, prompt caching, modular prompts and Skills. Where this chapter touches caching (a stable prompt prefix is cacheable), it points there.
  • Chapter 11 owns evaluation methodology. Here you meet only enough of it to make a selection and release decision.
  • Chapter 13 owns the guardrail and human-in-the-loop design in full, and chapter 14 owns the compliance regimes. This chapter places guardrails in layers and shows which rules the prompt may carry.
  • Chapter 02 owns workflow and agent patterns, and chapter 03 owns multi-agent decomposition. A router in this chapter is a model-selection device, not an orchestration pattern.
  • The foundations-level mechanics of prompting (explicit criteria, few-shot construction, structured output and retry) are in the CCAR-F chapters 11 and 12. They are not repeated here.
7e1cd4f154:
Telephone self-service started with touch-tone menus: press 1 for billing.

Speech recognition arrived in the 1990s as hand-written grammars. A grammar was a list of phrases the recogniser would accept at each prompt. The web era standardised them in VoiceXML (a W3C submission in 2000, a Recommendation in 2004) and in the speech-recognition grammar specification that came with it.

A grammar is a closed set. It is precise, testable and fast. And it fails the moment a caller says something the author did not foresee. The classic IVR failure ("I'm sorry, I didn't get that") is the grammar's coverage boundary.

Intent classification with a language model replaces the closed set with an open one. In doing so it trades a deterministic coverage hole for a probabilistic error rate.

The requirement language of the old world survives intact. The call-flow designer's table of intents, their volumes and their target recognition rates is exactly the per-segment requirement this chapter keeps asking for.
57b3924292:
The twelve-factor app methodology was published by the Heroku engineers around 2011. It said that anything that varies between deployments belongs in configuration, strictly separated from code. It also said the build, release and run stages should be separate.

Semantic Versioning 2.0.0 (2013) gave teams a shared way to say what kind of change a new version is. Infrastructure as code followed, and so did the GitOps habit of reviewing a diff before a change reaches production.

A system prompt is configuration in this sense. It changes behaviour without changing code, so it needs the same treatment: review, version, promotion and rollback. Teams that kept prompts as string literals scattered across services, or edited them in a web console, rediscovered every problem the twelve-factor authors described.
49a9db29d1:
Saltzer and Schroeder's 1975 paper "The Protection of Information in Computer Systems" set out design principles that still read as a checklist for guardrails:

  • fail-safe defaults (deny unless permitted);
  • complete mediation (check every access);
  • least privilege;
  • separation of privilege;
  • economy of mechanism.

James Reason's Swiss cheese model of accidents, from his 1990 book on human error, added the picture most architects carry. Every layer of defence has holes. A failure happens when the holes line up. So the aim is independent layers, not one perfect one.

Prompt injection was named and widely discussed from September 2022 onward. The term is usually credited to Simon Willison (check the original posts for dates). The OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications, first published in 2023, put it at the head of its list.

The lesson for this chapter is the old one. A probabilistic component is one slice of cheese, and the slices that must not have holes are made of code.
41185bf161:
Cascaded classifiers are older than language models. The Viola and Jones face detector (2001) ran a cheap test first and passed only the ambiguous windows to more expensive tests. That made real-time detection affordable.

The same idea appeared for large language models in the FrugalGPT paper (Chen, Zaharia and Zou, 2023). It studied sending a query to cheaper models first and escalating when a scorer judged the answer unreliable. On the benchmarks it used, it reported large cost reductions at comparable accuracy.

The cost saving is real. So is the dependency it exposes: everything rests on the scorer. A cascade is only as good as its acceptance check, which is why section 08 spends time on what makes a trustworthy one.
07515778c4:
The GPT-3 paper "Language Models are Few-Shot Learners" (Brown and colleagues, 2020) showed that a large pretrained model could pick up a task from a handful of examples placed in its context. No weight update was needed.

"Chain-of-Thought Prompting Elicits Reasoning in Large Language Models" (Wei and colleagues, 2022) showed that writing out intermediate steps in the examples improved accuracy on multi-step problems. The same year, Kojima and colleagues reported that a plain instruction such as "Let's think step by step" gave a smaller version of the gain, without any examples.

Current Claude models can reason before answering through built-in thinking. That moved the technique out of the prompt and into a request setting.

The engineering lesson did not change. Each technique helps some tasks, costs tokens and seconds, and does nothing for others. That is why section 13 treats technique as a variable in an experiment, not as a belief.
f6ad180d67:
Selecting a model means choosing values for four variables at once. The exam's scenarios are built by tightening one of them until a naive design breaks.

  • quality is not a single number. It is a table with one accuracy (or pass rate, or grader score) per segment. A requirement is written per segment ("95 percent on each of 14 intents"), and an average hides the weak row.
  • latency is a distribution measured at a percentile. It has two parts: a time to first token that you cannot control much, and a generation time proportional to the number of output tokens.
  • cost scales with tokens in and tokens out. Output tokens (including any reasoning tokens) are the expensive side on every tier.
  • operational risk is what a wrong answer costs, how it is detected and who can reverse it. It decides how much of the decision can be automated and where the human gate sits.
cc1c91b67f:
The tiers differ along all four.

A larger model has more capacity for multi-step reasoning, for following many simultaneous constraints, and for judgement on ambiguous input. It costs more per token and generates tokens more slowly.

A smaller model is cheaper and faster. On a narrow, well-specified task it is frequently indistinguishable from the larger one: classification into a fixed set of labels, extraction into a fixed schema, a short rewrite. That sentence is the whole economic argument for tiers. The word "frequently" is the reason you measure.

Carry the ratio between tiers in your head. With the placeholder prices used here, the mid tier costs three times the small tier per token, and the large tier five times. And a call that generates twelve times as many output tokens costs about twelve times as much on the output side, regardless of tier.
92bfeb7cb2:
Read the first three rows as shapes. The ratios produce the decisions in the rest of this chapter: 3x and 5x on price, a first-token time several times larger, and a generation speed a third as fast.

The absolute values change with every release. An answer on the exam never depends on them. It depends on whether you applied the ratios to the numbers in the scenario.

The identifiers, the context-window sizes, whether a tier supports an effort setting or adaptive thinking, and the current prices are product facts. Check the docs, and write the date you looked into the selection record.
f94f43ba47:
The last line is the selection rule. It has the shape of an elimination followed by a minimisation: drop every configuration that violates a hard constraint, then take the cheapest of what remains.

Exam distractors encode the mistake of running it the other way round. They pick the most accurate configuration and then ask whether it is affordable. Or they weight accuracy against latency as if the SLA were a preference.

An SLA is a constraint, not a weight (chapter 01, section 13). An accuracy floor is a constraint too. Past the floor, extra accuracy buys nothing the requirement asked for.
5a7e12d632:
Model selection is load testing for quality. A Spring architect sizing a service does not pick an instance type from a brochure. She runs the service on candidate sizes and picks the smallest that meets the p95 target with headroom.

The same procedure applies here, in five steps you can recite:

  1. Write the requirement per segment. The card from chapter 01 already has it.
  2. Build the labelled set before any prompt is tuned, stratified so every segment has enough cases to be judged. Chapter 11 gives the sample sizes. For a single 95 percent floor, a segment needs on the order of 60 clean cases just to rule out a failing rate, and several hundred to rule out a rate near the floor.
  3. Run every candidate tier with the same prompt. Record accuracy by segment, latency percentiles and cost per call.
  4. Choose the cheapest configuration that passes every segment inside every constraint.
  5. Record the result with the date, the prompt version and the identifiers. The answer expires when any of them changes.
062930f753:
The running example is the telecom IVR. Callers speak, a speech recogniser produces text, and a classifier assigns one of 14 intents: balance, payment, plan change, outage report, device upgrade, roaming, promotion question, bill dispute, port-in, SIM or eSIM, cancellation, address update, technical support, agent request.

The requirement card reads:

  • at least 95 percent accuracy on each intent;
  • a p95 of 680 milliseconds for the model step (the call has 800 milliseconds end to end, and 120 are spent in network, account lookup and post-processing; see section 03 and example 14);
  • at most $0.003 per call, at a volume of 2.4 million calls a month.

The primary pillar is the performance SLA. Cost is secondary.

The probe uses 300 cases per intent, 4,200 in all. The model is scripted so the example is repeatable. The accuracy values behind the script are invented. What matters is the shape of the report and what it forces you to see.
f6a8f736d9:
Look at what the report refuses to let you do.

The small tier has a 96.5 percent overall accuracy, which would clear a 95 percent aggregate bar. It is the cheapest, and the only tier that fits the latency budget. It is still out. Four intents are below 95 percent, and the worst, the promotion question, is at 88.0 percent.

The mid tier is better on every intent and still fails on two intents and on latency. The large tier clears every accuracy floor (its worst intent is at 97.0 percent). It fails on latency by more than a factor of two, and on cost.

No tier passes. A reader who sorts by accuracy picks the large tier and discovers in production that the IVR times out. They have bought a latency breach with a bill three times the ceiling.

The report's last line is the correct instruction: do not buy a bigger model; read the failing intents; fix the prompt.
a6ac64da1d:
Reading the failing intents takes about thirty minutes. It is the part of the job a notebook cannot do for you.

Pull twenty misclassified utterances for the promotion question and the bill dispute. On real data you would expect them to be mostly each other. A caller who says "I was promised twenty-five dollars a line and I'm paying thirty" is asking about a misapplied promotion. They are also disputing a charge. The prompt's two definitions overlap.

The remedy is a sharper definition and two boundary examples (section 12), not a larger model. Version v2 of the prompt adds them, and the probe is re-run with everything else held constant.
15cd69b3a5:
Now the small tier passes. Every intent is at or above 96.3 percent. The p95 is 554 milliseconds against 680. The cost is $0.0012 per call, which at 2.4 million calls is about $2,900 a month on the placeholder prices.

The mid tier is more accurate (its worst intent is 97.3 percent). But it costs about three times as much and misses the budget. The large tier would cost about $14,000 a month.

The decision is the small tier with prompt v2, and the arithmetic for rejecting the others is on the record.

One more line in the output deserves attention. The lowest Wilson lower bound across intents is 93.6 percent. That is under the floor, even though the point estimate for every intent is above it. With 300 cases per intent the interval is wide. So the correct statement is that the small tier looks sufficient, and a shadow-mode week on live traffic (chapter 01, section 17) should confirm it before cut-over.

The same approach handles a rare intent with only a few hundred monthly calls, where no probe will ever give a tight interval. Launch it behind a human fallback and let production data tighten the estimate.
77b29d9fff:
Here is the harness in code, written against the real API so you can point it at your own labelled set. Three details matter more than the loop.

  • The same system prompt is used for every tier. The comparison is of tiers, not of prompts.
  • The result keeps accuracy per segment. The choice function returns the first tier, cheapest first, that passes everything.
  • When nothing passes, the function returns nothing and says why. That is the behaviour that stops a reflexive upgrade.

The companion version of this function runs against the scripted client, so you can execute it offline.
cc18efc4b0:
In Java, this gate is a build step, not a notebook. A nightly job writes the probe results to a JSON file. A parameterised test fails the build when any segment is under its floor.

That way a prompt change, a model-identifier change or a data refresh cannot reach production while a segment is red. It is the same discipline that stops a failing unit test from being merged.
0296ed8a5a:
When the cheapest tier does not pass, moving up a tier is not the only way to close the gap. The order in which you try the options is a matter of cost and risk.

  • A prompt change costs an afternoon and is reversible in one step. If it works, it lowers no margin.
  • Spending more reasoning on the hard requests (higher effort, or thinking turned on) costs output tokens and seconds on every call that uses it.
  • Moving deterministic work out of the model and into code removes tokens, latency and a source of error, all at once.
  • Moving to a larger tier raises price and latency on every call. As example 01 just showed, it can break a constraint that was holding.

So the ladder runs: fix the prompt and the labels, then spend reasoning where the eval shows it pays, then move arithmetic and lookups into code, then change tier. The exam rewards the candidate who can say why each rung comes before the next, with a number.
8f387f2926:
The second dial inside a tier needs a precise description, because candidates confuse its parts.

Thinking lets the model generate reasoning tokens before it answers. Later tokens can condition on the intermediate results. That is why it helps with multi-step problems such as proration across a mid-cycle plan change. Reasoning tokens are billed as output, the expensive side, and they take generation time. A response with 1,200 reasoning tokens on a mid tier at 95 tokens per second spends about 12 seconds on thinking alone.

Effort is a coarser signal about how much work to put into the whole response. It covers how deeply to think, how verbose to be and how many tool calls to make.

The exact request fields differ by model generation. At the time of writing, the larger tiers expose an effort setting and an adaptive form of thinking in which the model decides when to think. An explicit token budget for thinking is the older form. Check the docs for the parameter names, the tiers that support each, and the defaults.

Two behaviours are stable enough to design around. A thinking budget or effort level is a signal, not a guarantee of a particular amount of reasoning. And max_tokens is a hard cap on everything generated, thinking included. A large reasoning allowance with a small cap truncates the answer.
fec1f1572c:
The task for the ladder is the outage-credit computation that section 14 builds in full. Given a customer, an outage record and a policy, decide which credit rule applies and compute the amount. There are four credit types: full outage, partial outage, degraded service, multi-day.

The card says at least 98 percent on every type, a p95 of 8 seconds for the whole reply (streaming shows the first words much sooner), and at most $0.010 per request.

Six configurations were measured. The accuracy figures are invented. The cost and p95 columns come from the token counts and the latency model.
e1f2765905:
Walk down the rows.

  • Configuration A, the small tier with the first prompt, is cheap and wrong on multi-day credits (80.0 percent).
  • B fixes the policy wording, which was ambiguous about whether a four-hour degradation counts as a day, and adds two boundary examples. The small tier improves to 88.0 percent and stops there. That tells you the remaining errors are about reasoning, not wording.
  • C moves to the mid tier at low effort: 94.0 percent on multi-day, still short.
  • D turns on high effort with thinking and reaches the floor (98.0 percent). But it generates 1,200 tokens, takes a p95 of 18.4 seconds and costs $0.0205 a request. That is over the SLA and over the ceiling.
  • E is the interesting one. It keeps the mid tier and high effort but changes the division of labour: the model decides which rule applies and which inputs matter, and code does the proration arithmetic. Output falls to 400 tokens, the p95 to 6.7 seconds and the cost to $0.0085. The worst type is 98.2 percent.
  • F, the large tier at medium effort, also passes accuracy. It fails the SLA and the ceiling by a factor of two to three.
f5ed552994:
Two lessons carry.

First, the winning rung was not on the "model" axis at all. Moving the arithmetic into code is the highest-value change in the table. It removes the cost, and it removes the failure mode too: a language model summing prorated days is a way to produce confident, small errors. The hybrid split of chapter 01, section 16 applies inside a model-facing step too.

Second, the accuracy floor, the SLA and the cost ceiling each eliminated at least one configuration, and cost chose the survivor. If the SLA had been 20 seconds, D would have been out on cost alone. If the ceiling had been $0.03, F would have survived, and the decision would have fallen to latency headroom. Write the three constraints next to the table and the choice follows.
4d4ddbc981:
Few systems have one task. A retail returns assistant answers order-status questions and produces return labels. It explains the policy on opened electronics. Now and then it arbitrates a dispute about a damaged item bought with a gift card and two coupons.

On the placeholder prices, running all of that on the large tier costs $0.0125 for a typical 1,000-input, 300-output turn. The small tier costs $0.0025. If 78 percent of the traffic is the kind the small tier handles, an all-large design pays five times the price on three quarters of the volume.

Two patterns exist to avoid that. The exam expects you to tell them apart by what each one depends on.
3d9aaa020b:
A router classifies the request first and dispatches it to a fixed tier. The classifier can be rules (the channel, the intent code the IVR already produced, the customer segment, the document type, the length of the input), an embedding classifier, or a small-model call.

A rules router adds no latency and no cost. A small-model router adds one short call, about 300 input and 10 output tokens, which on the placeholder prices is $0.00035.

Its failure mode is misrouting. Send a complex dispute to the small tier and you have a confident wrong answer. So the router is a classifier like any other. It has a confusion matrix, a floor per class, and a defined direction for its errors. When unsure, it should route up a tier. Sending a simple request to a larger tier costs cents. The opposite costs a wrong answer.
42f69eb4f2:
A cascade tries the cheap tier first and escalates when an acceptance check rejects the answer. It needs no up-front classification, so it handles the case where difficulty only shows after trying.

It depends entirely on the check. A trustworthy check does not share the generator's blind spots. Examples are a schema validation, a deterministic business rule over the output and the account facts, a second-pass verifier call, an explicit field in which the model reports that it needs help, or agreement across several samples. The untrustworthy check is the one most often proposed: the model's own stated confidence, which section 07 measures.

Cascades also carry a latency cost that a brochure leaves out. A request that fails the first rung pays for two calls and two waits. The tail of the latency distribution is the sum, so the escalated fraction alone can violate a strict p95.
525eaa80cf:
The economic comparison between them is a one-line inequality. It is worth deriving, because it tells you what to measure.

Let the small and mid costs per turn be cs and cm. Let h be the share of traffic that needs the mid tier, and cr the router call. Let e be the cascade's escalation rate (true rejections plus false rejections).

The router costs cr + (1−h)cs + h cm. The cascade costs cs + e cm. The cascade is cheaper when e < h − (h cs − cr)/cm.

With the numbers above (h = 0.22, cs = $0.0025, cm = $0.0075, cr = $0.00035), the break-even escalation rate is about 19 percent. If your check rejects more than about one answer in five, a router is cheaper, and it has no tail problem.

The inequality ignores quality. That is where the next output earns its place.
77a6a76a61:
Read the output in three passes.

The single-tier rows establish the problem. The small tier is 96.0 percent blended but 70.0 percent on the complex class. That class is 3 percent of traffic, and probably the 3 percent that generates the escalations and the complaints. The large tier is 96.0 percent on the complex class and costs five times the small one.

The router rows keep the complex class at the large tier's 96.0 percent when the router is perfect. When it misroutes 15 percent of the complex cases one tier down, the class drops to 94.8 percent. Both cost roughly a third of the all-large design.

The cascade rows are cheaper still (about $0.0031 to $0.0035 a turn). Their worst class is far more sensitive to the check. With a strong check that catches 90 percent of wrong answers, the complex class reaches 93.7 percent. With a check that catches 60 percent, it falls to 83.5 percent, and with 30 percent to 75.1 percent.

The escalation rates (7 to 11 percent) are under the 19 percent break-even in all three. So the cascade wins on cost in every row. The question the architect must answer is whether the check's catch rate has been measured. If it has not, the router is the safer design.
1609c40db7:
A latency note that connects to the IVR. The 680 millisecond model-step budget leaves no room for a model-based router, or for a second rung on escalation. Even the small tier uses 554 milliseconds at p95 for a bare label.

In that system the routing happens before the classification call, by rules: the dialled number, the account status, whether the caller is authenticated. The cascade, if any, is a human fallback.

Routing and cascades are a tool for chat, email and back-office traffic whose SLA is measured in seconds. An exam item that offers a two-rung model cascade for a sub-second voice step is testing whether you checked the budget.
3ddfe5384f:
The most common proposal for a cascade's acceptance check is to ask the model how confident it is, and escalate below a threshold. It is attractive because it costs nothing extra, and because humans read "92 percent" as a probability.

Whether it is one is an empirical question about a specific model, prompt and task. You answer it with a reliability table. A weather forecaster's "30 percent chance of rain" is checked the same way: count how often it rained on days that got 30 percent.

Scoring probabilistic forecasts against outcomes goes back to Brier's 1950 paper on forecast verification. The reliability diagram and the expected calibration error became standard ways to report it. Guo and colleagues' 2017 study of modern neural networks used them and found the networks were often overconfident. Work on language models (for example Kadavath and colleagues, 2022) reports that stated probabilities can be reasonably calibrated in some formats and not in others.

The architect's position is to assume nothing and measure.
c741c9d225:
The scripted small tier here is wrong 3.3 percent of the time. Its stated confidence is high on both right and wrong answers. The reliability table shows bins whose mean stated confidence is 0.85 and whose measured accuracy is 98.8 percent. It also shows a bin at 0.7 to 0.8 that is only 89 percent accurate. So the score is informative, but it is not a probability (expected calibration error 0.095).

Now look at what a threshold buys.

  • At 0.80 the cascade escalates 10.9 percent of calls and catches 57.0 percent of the wrong answers, wasting 9.3 percent of the right ones.
  • To catch three quarters of the wrong answers (a threshold of 0.90), it must escalate 57.1 percent of all traffic. Of that, 56.6 points are right answers re-asked at a larger tier.
  • At 0.95 it escalates four calls in five.

A cascade that escalates that much has no cost advantage over the larger tier, and its mean latency is worse.

The rule check in the last row of the table has an invented catch rate of 62 percent and a false-reject rate of 1 percent. It escalates 3.3 percent of calls and catches 65.8 percent of the wrong answers. That is the shape of a trigger worth building.
bd0ee01c16:
Here is the alternative written as code, and it is deliberately boring. The acceptance function is deterministic, cheap and aware of the business. It checks that:

  • the output parses;
  • the label is one of the allowed values;
  • the amount is within the disputed amount;
  • the account in the output is the account in the request.

Every rung failure moves to the next tier. The last rung is a person, not a larger prompt. The model may also volunteer that it cannot decide (the needs_escalation field), and that signal is honoured, not weighted.
0078550f35:
Where a self-reported score is all you have, there is a defensible way to use it.

  1. Measure the reliability table on a labelled set for the exact model, prompt and output format you will run.
  2. Fit a calibration map if it helps. The simplest is a per-bin lookup of measured accuracy.
  3. Set the threshold from the cost model, not from a round number.
  4. Re-run the table after every model or prompt change. The score's meaning moves with both.
  5. Track the escalation rate in production as an alarm. A rate that doubles overnight after a vendor-side model update is a calibration shift announcing itself.
c210d7fa53:
A model upgrade is a dependency upgrade. A prompt edit is a configuration change that alters behaviour with no compile step to catch it. Both reach production through the same door. Teams that treated them casually learned the lesson an engineer learns the first time a transitive dependency changes on a Friday.

Four disciplines handle it.

  • Pin: configuration names one exact model identifier and one exact prompt version, and the code refuses an alias that can move. Whether a given identifier is a fixed snapshot or an alias the provider re-points is a product detail (check the docs for the identifier scheme and the deprecation policy). Your configuration check should reject anything you cannot show is fixed.
  • Gate: a candidate (new model, new prompt, new settings) is evaluated against the baseline on the same labelled set, per segment, before anyone sees it.
  • Canary: a small, sticky slice of live traffic runs the candidate while the baseline serves the rest.
  • Roll back: the previous pinned pair is one configuration change away, and rolling back is rehearsed.
8f8d5540ad:
Take the gate first. The exam's favourite item is a model upgrade that improves the headline number. A new small-tier model scores better on the overall metric, and the vendor's notes say it is stronger across the board.

The gate does not read the vendor's notes. It reads the per-segment table. Example 12 runs two candidates against the baseline on the eight intents with the most business weight. The first is a model upgrade. The second is a prompt change that adds boundary examples for the two weakest intents.
0bc05e1708:
The model upgrade improves four intents by 1.0 to 2.2 points. The overall (equal-weighted) accuracy rises from 98.0 to 98.6 percent. It also takes cancellations from 97.0 percent to 93.0 percent. That is under the 95 percent floor, and the two-proportion test calls the 4-point drop significant (z = −2.6 at 400 cases per arm).

The decision is to block, keep the baseline pinned, and send the regression back to the prompt owner. The improvement elsewhere is real. It is a reason to fix the cancellation section and try again, not a reason to ship. Cancellation is exactly the intent the retention team cares about most. A model that is slightly better everywhere and worse there is a worse model for this business.

The second candidate changes one variable (the prompt). It improves the two weak intents by 1.3 to 1.7 points, regresses nothing, and is promoted to a canary.

Two rules from the gate carry over to your own. The floor applies per segment, and the overall number never overrides a failing segment. And a drop is judged against noise: a one-point wobble on 400 cases does not block a release, while a four-point drop does.
ce2d441245:
Release one variable at a time. If the model identifier and the prompt version change in the same release and a segment moves, you do not know which one moved it. Keep them as separate keys in configuration and change them in separate releases. Then the rollback of either is a single edit.

The configuration below is the shape to aim for. The prompt reference points at an entry in the registry of section 10. The canary block names its own model and prompt. The percentage is zero by default.
d52bbf93f7:
The canary has a property that is easy to get wrong, and the exam probes it: stickiness.

Suppose each request flips a coin. A customer in the middle of a four-turn conversation can be served by two model versions. The arms are mixed, so the comparison between them becomes meaningless. And a customer who sees the assistant's tone change mid-chat files a complaint.

The fix is to derive the arm from the identity of the customer or the conversation by hashing it. Raising the percentage should only add accounts, never remove them, so an account in the 5 percent cohort is still in the 25 percent cohort. Example 13 verifies both properties and measures what random assignment does to journeys.
bdc842e781:
With the placeholder seed, random assignment at a 5 percent canary showed both versions to 18.7 percent of four-turn journeys. The hash bucket gives zero by construction. The cohort sizes land within a few hundredths of a point of target, and every account in the 5 percent canary stays in at 25 percent.

Use a salt per experiment. If two experiments use the same bucketing, the same customers are always in both canaries, and the effects are confounded.
ff23f6c31b:
The system prompt is the part of the context that stays constant across a conversation and across customers. It tells the model who it is in this application, what it may and may not do, how to treat the inputs it will see, and what shape its outputs take.

For a Spring architect, the useful mental model is the split between configuration and request payload. Configuration is stable, reviewed, versioned and shared. Payload is variable and per-request. Where it contains customer text or retrieved documents, it is untrusted. The system prompt is configuration.

Two consequences follow, and the exam tests both.

First, per-request data (the account number, today's date, the customer's balance) does not belong in it. It makes the prompt differ for every call, defeats prompt caching on the stable prefix (chapter 05), and mixes data with instructions.

Second, the system prompt is not a security boundary. It states policy so the model behaves well. But a determined user can argue with it, which is why section 11 enforces the rules that matter somewhere else.
7b5f704f0c:
Within the prompt, structure is a maintenance tool as much as a model-facing one. Anthropic's prompting guidance recommends separating sections with XML-style tags (check the docs for the current guidance). The practical benefit is that the model, the reviewers and your tooling can all refer to a section by name: "follow the rules in the policy section".

A workable skeleton has six parts, each with one job:

  • the role (who, for whom, in what tone);
  • the success criteria (what a good answer is);
  • the policy (what the model may do, must not do, and when it escalates);
  • guidance on tools (when to call which);
  • the output format (schema, length, citation style);
  • examples (section 12).

The request context follows it: the retrieved documents, account facts and the customer's message. That goes in the user turn, in its own tagged blocks.
af38054a05:
Three rules make a prompt like this maintainable.

First, give the reason when it is not obvious. "Credits above $50 go to a human because approval limits are a finance control" does two jobs. The model generalises better from a reason than from a bare command: it will route a $60 goodwill gesture correctly without a separate rule. And the next reviewer can tell whether the rule is still needed, because the reason names the control it implements.

Second, state rules plainly and specifically instead of in capitals. A prompt in which every line says ALWAYS or NEVER teaches the model that everything is equally urgent. In practice it produces over-application: refusals of legitimate requests, and rigid behaviour in cases the author never meant to cover.

Third, one prompt per job. A single six-thousand-word prompt that serves five products and three channels accumulates contradictions. Every edit becomes a risk to every product. It cannot be cached or reviewed in pieces. Split it into modules assembled per route (chapter 05).
9ce0f96bcb:
Parts of this review can be automated, and should be. A lint that runs on every pull request catches the defects a tired reviewer misses.

Example 07 checks for missing sections, shouted rules, rules without reasons, hard limits stated only in prose, per-request data in the stable prompt, and size. It is heuristic and cheap. It proves nothing about behaviour; that is the evaluation's job. Still, it flags the same things a good reviewer flags.
f74a005003:
The mega-prompt fails seven checks: no sections, four shouted rules, six rules with no stated reason, two hard limits that exist only as prose, and an account number and a date baked into text that was supposed to be stable.

The sectioned version passes all of them, including the hard-limit check, because each limit carries a note saying where it is also enforced.

When the lint finds a hard limit in prose with no enforcement note, ask a question: where does this rule actually hold? For money, privacy and law, the answer belongs in section 11.
d35813c807:
A template is the system prompt plus the structure of the user turn, with named slots for the variable content. Once the prompt is configuration, the template is the thing you release. So you ask the questions you would ask of any release artifact:

  • Which version is running?
  • Who changed it, and who approved it?
  • What evidence says it works?
  • Can I get the previous one back in one step?
  • Could someone have edited it in place without anyone knowing?

A directory of text files in the application repository answers some of those. It answers all of them only if you add four properties, which the registry in example 05 shows.

  • Versions are immutable. A published version never changes, and a change is a new version.
  • Each version carries a content hash recorded at approval. The loader recomputes it and refuses a mismatch.
  • Approval requires evidence. The registry will not mark a version approved unless an evaluation report is attached and every segment clears the floor.
  • Callers pin an exact version or a promoted alias, and the loader rejects "latest".
178c1d324b:
Walk the output as a story.

Version 7 is registered, but its evaluation has two segments at 88.0 and 90.0 percent. So approval is refused, and pointing production at a draft is refused for the same reason.

Version 8 carries boundary examples, clears the floor, and is approved and promoted. Overwriting version 8 fails: the history is append-only. Asking for "latest" fails: callers cannot float.

Resolving the production alias works, until someone edits the file by hand after approval. Then the hash check refuses to serve it. That last check is not paranoia. It is how you find the console edit made at 2 a.m. during an incident and never committed.

Finally, promoting version 9 records the previous version on the alias. Rollback is a lookup, not an investigation.
0c2f99deef:
The second half of the template is the rendering. That is where the security-relevant mistakes happen. A prompt built by string concatenation has three failure modes:

  • a missing variable renders as an empty section, which the model then fills with its own guesses;
  • a typo in a slot name silently drops a value;
  • untrusted text can contain the closing tag of its own block, followed by text that looks like instructions.

A strict renderer closes all three. Every slot is declared with a size cap. Missing and extra values are errors raised at build time. Angle brackets and ampersands in untrusted values are escaped, so a value cannot close a tag it sits inside.

None of this makes prompt injection impossible. It removes the cheapest attacks and keeps the structure honest. The real defence against injection is the layered one of section 11.
d1f97e55fb:
In a Spring service the loader is a bean. The hash check is part of startup, so a bad artifact fails the deployment instead of the first customer.

The same class is the natural place to refuse a prompt whose recorded model differs from the one configured for the role. That catches a prompt that was tuned and evaluated on one tier and is now running on another.
2b5dbe7418:
A guardrail is anything that keeps the system's behaviour inside its allowed envelope. The design question is which mechanism holds which rule. The answer follows from one distinction.

A reducing control lowers the probability of a bad outcome but cannot rule it out. An enforcing control makes the bad outcome impossible for the cases it covers.

A system prompt is a reducing control. A model follows it with high probability. The exceptions are rare, unpredictable and occasionally induced by an adversary.

Some controls enforce: a tool that rejects an amount over a limit, a data-access layer that never returns another customer's records, a logger that redacts before writing. Their behaviour does not depend on what a model decides.

The rule of thumb the exam rewards is short. If a violation costs money, breaks a law, or leaks data, enforce it below the prompt. Keep the prompt statement too, so the model behaves well first time.
22a7f43e76:
Here are the layers, in the order a request meets them.

  • Input controls run before the model: size caps, redaction of data the model does not need, and the decision about what data to fetch at all. They also screen for known injection patterns, as a signal that removes tools or flags the turn, not as a promise.
  • Prompt controls are the policy in the system prompt: scope, tone, escalation rules, and the instruction to treat quoted text as data.
  • Tool controls sit between the model's intent and the world: authentication and authorisation against the calling customer, hard limits, schema validation, idempotency keys, and error messages that tell the model what to do next.
  • Output controls inspect what is about to reach the customer: schema validity, a scan for identifiers that must not leave, a requirement that claims carry a citation, and a block on commitments the business has not approved.
  • Human controls own the middle band: approval above a threshold, sampled review, and an appeal path.

This is Reason's Swiss cheese applied. The layers are meant to have independent holes. A control that depends on the model's cooperation cannot be the only one for a rule that must hold.
f0bdbc1715:
One layer deserves a warning, because it looks like code and behaves like a model. That is the classifier or "judge" model used as a guardrail, for example a small-tier call that screens each reply for tone or topic.

It is useful for soft rules, where an occasional miss is a quality defect that sampling will find. But it is probabilistic. It has its own error rates, and it costs a call and some latency. A hard rule that depends on a model-based guardrail alone has the same weakness as the same rule in the prompt, one step removed.

Evaluate such a guardrail like any classifier: its catch rate and false-reject rate, per category. And keep it away from limits, authorisation and privacy.
b813d921dd:
Example 09 puts a number on the argument for the credit limit. It simulates two million credit requests in which 3 percent of customers ask for more than the $50 limit, so about 60,000 over-limit asks. It varies the probability that the model proposes an over-limit credit anyway.

The probabilities are invented. The point is the shape: wording and examples shrink the leak and never remove it.
b20d3485aa:
With plain wording the model leaks 493 over-limit credits (0.8 percent of 60,118 asks). Shouting reduces that to 183. Six few-shot examples reduce it to 98. Only the tool brings it to zero.

Ninety-eight leaked credits in a simulated period is ninety-eight audit findings, against a control that is supposed to hold for every transaction. Stronger prompting is a reasonable thing to do. It is not a control.

The same reasoning answers a very common exam item: a credit agent sometimes exceeds a policy limit despite a clear instruction. Better wording, more examples and a larger model are all distractors, because each one leaves a financial control probabilistic. The fix is to enforce the limit in the tool and return an error that tells the model what to do next. Then a rejection becomes a correct escalation, not a confused retry loop.
6b8b27bbe5: A guardrail is a promise, and a promise needs a test. Example 08 runs ten scripted scenarios through all five layers and records which layer stopped each problem. The problems include a credit above the limit, a credit against another customer's account, an injected instruction, an SSN in a reply, an uncited claim and an unapproved promise. Then it removes one layer at a time to see what escapes.
100b79856c:
No scenario escapes the full stack. The ablation is the educational part.

  • Without the tool layer, two scenarios reach the ledger: the over-limit credit and the credit against the wrong account.
  • Without the output layer, five reach the customer.
  • Without the human gate, the $40 credit that needs approval is executed unapproved.
  • Without the input layer or the prompt layer, nothing escapes in this suite, because the tool and output layers back them up.

That last result is the correct lesson, and it is easy to misread. The input and prompt layers are not decoration. They cut how often the backstops fire. A backstop that fires on every tenth request means a poor customer experience and a noisy alert stream. But they are not what you rely on for a rule that must hold. Know which layers enforce.
a7818d79dc:
Finally, turn the promises into a regression suite that runs on every prompt, model and tool change. Example 16 does this against the real loop shape with a scripted model. Six unit tests assert that:

  • a request for a human results in an escalation;
  • an over-limit credit never reaches the ledger;
  • a credit for another customer's account is refused;
  • text injected into a document cannot widen authorisation;
  • a tool error steers the model to escalation;
  • a legitimate credit goes through.

Against the real API, the same tests run N times and track a pass rate. A probabilistic behaviour has a rate, not a verdict (chapter 11). The point of writing them first is that each one is a sentence from the policy.
257ef54f27:
Chapters 11 and 12 of the foundations guide teach how to write explicit criteria and construct few-shot examples. At the professional level the questions change. Which technique does this task need? What does it cost per call at this volume? How do you know? And where does it live in the release process?

The three techniques convey what you want in different ways.

  • Zero-shot gives instructions only.
  • Few-shot adds worked examples, typically three to five, wrapped in tags so the model reads them as examples and not as part of the conversation.
  • Reasoning before answering (thinking, or an explicit instruction and a place to write the reasoning) lets the model produce intermediate results that later tokens can use.

They are not rival schools. A production system uses all three, on different steps.
2e6b3e14e6:
Zero-shot is the starting point. Current models follow clear instructions well, and the shortest prompt is the cheapest and the easiest to maintain. It is enough when the task is common, the criteria are precise and a schema constrains the output. It fails at fuzzy boundaries, where the model draws the line somewhere plausible that is not where your business draws it.

Few-shot examples communicate boundaries, format and tone better than prose can. They are only as good as their diversity. Four tidy variants of one situation teach the model to copy surface features such as length and phrasing. They teach it nothing about the boundary.

Reasoning helps where the answer depends on a chain of intermediate results: proration across a plan change, deciding which of three overlapping promotions applies, reconciling an event log against a credit rule. It is wasted on a lookup or a label. And it costs output tokens and seconds on every call that uses it.
193f8b7dc8: The architect's move is to treat the technique as a variable in the evaluation, per task, with the task's own floor and latency budget. Example 10 does this for three tasks with invented measurements: the IVR intent classifier, the bill-proration step, and invoice field extraction with a strict format.
cd211a5d1f:
Three tasks, three different winners.

The IVR classifier needs boundary examples. Zero-shot is at 91.2 percent on its worst intent, and five examples bring it to 96.2 percent. Thinking contributes nothing measurable (91.5 percent) while adding five seconds to a 0.8 second budget.

Invoice extraction also wants examples. Its failures are format and boundary failures. The example set takes the worst field from 97.5 to 99.2 percent, against a 99 percent floor.

Proration is the opposite. Examples barely move it (94.0 to 95.5 percent). Thinking moves it past the floor but misses the 8 second budget by several seconds. The technique that passes is to give the model a few examples and let code do the arithmetic. That reaches 98.8 percent at a p95 of 4.4 seconds.

This is the lever ladder again, seen from the technique side. The highest-value rung was not a prompt technique at all.
89d100db5e:
Examples are part of the versioned prompt, and they have maintenance problems that prose rules do not.

They drift from policy. A rule changes and an old example still shows the old behaviour, so the model gets contradictory evidence.

They cost tokens on every call. Take five boundary examples at about 700 tokens on a small tier, at the placeholder $1 per million input tokens, across 2.4 million calls a month. That is 1,680 million tokens: about $1,680 a month at full price, and about a tenth of that if the stable prefix is cached (chapter 05). It is cheap for the accuracy it buys in example 10, and worth stating in the record.

And they can be unrepresentative. Example 11 audits a set before it is committed. It checks pairwise similarity, label balance, coverage of the confusable pairs found in the confusion matrix, and agreement with the written rules.
b97ff44954:
Set A is four ways of saying "charged twice". Its mean similarity is not high by token overlap. But it uses one label, covers none of the three boundaries the eval found, and would teach nothing the instructions did not.

Set B was written from the confusion matrix, one pair of examples per boundary: a duplicate charge against a misapplied promotion, a third-party charge against a fraud report, a cancellation against a price complaint. It passes.

Set C is set B plus one example that contradicts a written rule: that a cancellation request outranks the billing question. The audit catches it. That is a real failure. An example is a more persuasive instruction than a sentence, and a contradiction between the two is resolved unpredictably.
862620b660:
Two cautions about reasoning.

First, thinking output is not an explanation to show a customer. Nor is it an audit record of why a decision was made. If you need an auditable rationale, ask for a structured field that cites the inputs used (the policy section and the numbers), and store that.

Second, when thinking is on, max_tokens must leave room for both the reasoning and the answer. Otherwise the response is truncated before it finishes.

Both are request-level details, so check the docs for how your model version reports and bills reasoning tokens.
bd0e533c8d:
A high-value architecture practice pattern is an aggregate that hides a segment-level failure. The guide-authored scenario sets a 95 percent requirement for each contract type, with an overall target of 96 percent. A system at 96 percent overall with one contract type at 91 percent fails. The correct response is to measure per type and fix any type below 95 percent before launch.

Read every requirement as written: the segment key, the metric, the percentile, the threshold and the direction.
c96c0f4b1b:
Notice three things about those requirements.

They carry a segment key: intent, credit type, reason code, contract type, alarm class. The key must exist in the data before the first test. That is a task for the discovery work of chapters 01 and 15.

They carry a metric chosen for the cost of error. Accuracy for the intents. Recall for the severity-1 alarms, because a missed alarm costs more than a false page. A rate of wrong refunds for the retail case.

And they carry a percentile for latency and a ceiling for cost. Together these define the region the design must live in.

A candidate who restates the requirement in those terms before choosing a design has done most of the work.
18bf1cc814:
Situation. A US carrier wants an assistant that handles outage-credit requests in chat. The card:

  • 400,000 requests a month;
  • credit decisions must match policy in at least 98 percent of cases for each of four credit types;
  • p95 of 8 seconds for the full reply;
  • $0.010 per request;
  • credits above $25 need human approval, and no credit above $50 is ever executed by the system.

The primary pillar is cost, with the SLA as a hard constraint. The alternative is a human tier that costs several dollars a contact.
ea86cc4307:
Step 1: decompose. The work splits into five parts:

  • extracting the account and the outage window from the customer's message;
  • looking up outage records for the cells that serve the customer;
  • deciding which credit rule applies (full or partial outage, degraded service, multi-day, caps per bill cycle);
  • computing the amount;
  • writing the reply.

Only two of those need a language model: extraction and the rule decision. Lookup and arithmetic are code (chapter 01, section 16). That alone removes the most error-prone step from the model.
f3de1a5210:
Step 2: measure per step. An extraction probe on the small tier gives (an invented figure) 99.1 percent, with a p95 of 420 milliseconds.

For the rule decision, the ladder of section 05 gives the answer:

  • the small tier is at 88.0 percent on the worst type, even after the prompt fix;
  • the mid tier with low effort is at 94.0 percent;
  • the mid tier with high effort and thinking reaches 98.0 percent, but its 1,200 reasoning tokens give a p95 of 18.4 seconds;
  • the mid tier at high effort, with code doing the proration, reaches 98.2 percent at 6.7 seconds.

The prompt fix mattered too. The policy was ambiguous on whether a four-hour degradation counts as a day. The clarified wording plus two boundary examples is what moved configuration A to B.
e2e4cae848:
The naive design costs $0.0270 a request. That is 2.7 times the ceiling, and $10,800 a month.

  • Caching the 2,400-token policy prefix, which is identical on every request, brings it to $0.0205.
  • Letting code do the sums cuts the output from 1,200 to 400 tokens and the cost to $0.0085.
  • Adding the small-tier extraction step makes it $0.0095. That is inside the ceiling with a 5 percent margin, or about $3,800 a month at 400,000 requests.

The large tier would cost $0.0164 for the decision step alone.

The chosen design is a two-model pipeline, a factor of three cheaper than the naive one. The margin is thin, though. A rise of a few percent in output length would put it over. So the cost meter of chapter 01 (section 14) belongs in the release plan.
4afa7c1eb6:
Step 4: governance designed in. The $50 limit and the account match live in the credit tool. The $25 approval band is a queue the tool writes to. The reply passes an output check that requires a policy citation and blocks any promise of an outcome.

Model identifiers and prompt versions are pinned in configuration. Each prompt has a registry entry, with an evaluation report attached to the approval. The six regression tests of section 11 run on every change.

Release is a sticky 5 percent canary for a week, with per-type accuracy sampled by QA. A probe alone cannot establish the 98 percent floor on the multi-day type: at 300 cases per type, its interval is wide.
b02ad9a9a3:
What the exam wants you to notice.

  • The decision is justified with per-type numbers.
  • The cheaper levers (prompt, caching, moving arithmetic into code) were tried before a bigger model.
  • The SLA and the ceiling each eliminated a design.
  • A two-model split was cheaper and more accurate than a single call.
  • Hard controls are in code.
  • The release is staged and reversible.
c1c9baddf2:
Governance in this chapter is not a separate workstream. It is four small artifacts that fall out of the design when you build it the way the preceding sections describe.

  • The selection record says what was chosen, against what requirement, on what evidence, with what alternatives rejected and why.
  • The prompt registry says which prompt version is approved, by what evaluation, with what content hash.
  • The release log says which model-and-prompt pair served which share of traffic in which period.
  • The per-call audit fields say which pair produced a particular output.

An auditor, a privacy officer or an incident reviewer asks one question in many forms. For this customer, on this date, which model, which prompt and which rules produced that decision? And what did we know about their accuracy at the time?

If those four artifacts exist, the answer takes a minute to find. If they do not, it takes a week, and the answer is a guess.
ae7043d12e: Generate the selection record; don't type it. Then it cannot drift from the numbers. Example 17 reads the requirement card, runs the probe from example 01 and writes the record in Markdown. It is deliberately short, and a reviewer can check every claim in it against a number.
3ae805a57d:
Three habits make a record like that useful in practice.

State the rejected alternatives with the measured reason: the mid tier fails the latency budget by 355 milliseconds and the cost ceiling by about 19 percent. Six months later someone will propose it again, and the record saves the argument.

Name the review trigger: any model or prompt change, and a quarterly re-run regardless. Model providers retire and replace models on a published schedule. A record with no review date describes a world that no longer exists.

And record the date and source of every price, since pricing is a product detail that changes.

The per-call fields below are what the observability stack of chapter 10 indexes. The point here is that the fields are decided at design time.
a658f9a563:
A last governance point belongs to this domain: the model's lifecycle is outside your control. Providers announce deprecations and retirements ahead of time (check the docs for the policy and for how far ahead). A retired model returns errors.

A planned migration that you started with a gate and a canary is a routine release. One that starts when production begins failing is an incident.

Put the retirement dates of every pinned model on a calendar. Keep the evaluation set and the harness runnable. Treat a deprecation notice as a ticket with a due date.
9d09b8182f: Building one big string with f-strings looks harmless. But it makes the system prompt unique per request, which defeats caching of the stable prefix. It mixes data with instructions. And it lets customer text close its own block.
a4b70351f7:
CCAR-P items give you figures and four plausible designs. The method that works:

  • (1) find the primary pillar;
  • (2) list the hard constraints (SLA percentile, per-segment floor, cost ceiling, compliance, approval bands);
  • (3) eliminate every option that violates one;
  • (4) among what remains, prefer the simplest design, and the one justified by a measurement.

Work each scenario before reading the reasoning. The wording of real items will differ, so treat these as practice for the reasoning, and check the official guide for the current format.
79964d9905:
The requirement is per intent, so A fails on four of them. B violates the latency budget by more than a factor of two, so it fails a hard constraint. D puts a second, slower call on a path that has 126 ms of headroom. It also relies on stated confidence, which example 04 shows is a weak trigger.

C follows the ladder. Two intents with overlapping definitions are a prompt defect, and the small tier passes every floor after the fix (96.3 percent on the worst intent, p95 554 ms). A lower Wilson bound under 95 percent also means a shadow-mode week before cut-over.
01d64ebac2:
The cost is a mix problem: the cheap 85 percent is paying large-tier prices.

A single move to the small tier (A) has no per-class evidence for the hard 15 percent. Shortening the prompt (B) addresses a variable that is not where a threefold excess comes from, and it is not an architecture answer. A discount (D) is commercial.

C is the router. It is built by rules first, because rules add no latency and no call. A per-class eval confirms each tier meets its floor, and errors have a defined direction (route up when unsure). Expect a blended cost of a third to a half of the all-large design on the placeholder ratios.
98032312a2:
Options A, B and D all leave a financial control probabilistic. Wording and examples lower the rate (example 09 shows 493, 183, 98 leaks and never zero). A larger model is still a model. A judge model has its own miss rate.

The control must hold for every transaction, so it belongs in code that does not depend on what the model decides. The error text steers the model to escalate_to_agent, so a rejection becomes a correct escalation. The prompt statement remains, so the model behaves well first time.
c4a96b80a9:
The floor is per segment, and the candidate is below it, with a drop the test calls significant.

B puts a known-failing segment in front of 5 percent of customers; the canary comes after the gate, not instead of it. D is unworkable, because intent is known only after classification.

C is the release discipline of section 08. The overall number never overrides a failing segment. One variable changes per release. And the baseline stays pinned, so rollback costs nothing.
b9987550e9:
At 0.9 the cascade pays the small tier plus the mid tier on 57 percent of traffic. That is well above the roughly 19 percent break-even against a router. And most of what it re-asks is already right (56.6 points of the 57.1).

Raising the threshold (C) escalates four calls in five. Lowering it (D) catches under a quarter of errors. The signal is informative but not calibrated, and using it costs more than it is worth.

B moves to a trigger that does not share the generator's blind spots, and measures it. With no such trigger, a router with a defined direction for its errors is the simpler design.
ed640a314a:
One change fixes two problems. A stable system prompt makes the policy prefix identical across customers, so it can be cached (chapter 05). And tagged, escaped blocks in the user turn remove the cheapest injection.

D helps a little, but it is a reducing control. Authorisation must live in the tools, and the pen test showed the prompt alone does not hold. A and B do not address the cause of either symptom.
7a3e0911db:
A fails the 8 s SLA, a hard constraint. B changes the tier without evidence that it moves the failing type. D relaxes a requirement without authority.

C removes the failure mode (model-performed arithmetic) and the cost of reasoning at once. In example 10 this configuration reaches 98.8 percent at a p95 of 4.4 s. It is also the pattern the exam favours generally: deterministic work in code, language in the model.
c0dac18a30: Done when: you can explain why each example's output leads to its decision. And, for a system of your own, you can state the per-segment floor, the cheapest passing tier, the lever that closed the gap, the rule enforced below the prompt, the pinned pair and the gate that protects it.
